newsitem.title: USA: US FCC issues satellite-TV public interest plan.
newsitem.headline: US FCC issues satellite-TV public interest plan.

text.p: The Federal Communications Commission issued an updated proposal Friday for imposing public-interest requirements on providers of direct broadcast statellite (DBS) television.

The agency's initial proposal, issued in 1993, was effectively frozen that same year after a U.S. federal court ruled that a section of the 1992 Cable Act was unconstitutional. The proposal stems from the act.
But last year a federal appeals court upheld the act's provision, paving the way for the FCC to reintroduce its DBS proposal.
The agency said that because of the three-year lag it wants to "update and refresh" its record on the proposal.

The Cable Act directs the FCC to impose on DBS providers the "equal time" provisions of federal communications law as well as the "reasonable access" provisions. Both relate to political candidates running for office.
The FCC is seeking comment on what "public interest or other requirements" should be imposed on DBS providers in addition to the equal time and reasonable access provisions.

In its 1993 proposal, the FCC tentatively concluded not to impose any added requirements, given that DBS was just in its infancy. "Should the rapid deployment of the DBS industry over the last several years, including technological advances that may in the near future allow DBS providers to offer some local programming, alter this conclusion," the FCC asked in its latest proposal.

The 1992 Cable Act also said a DBS provider must "reserve a portion of its channel capacity, equal to not less than four percent nor more than seven percent, exclusively for noncommercial programming of an educational and informational nature."
In its proposal, the FCC asked how the term "noncommercial" should be defined, among other matters.
